title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
objective: After this level you can explain how a shadow and a well let someone estimate Earth’s size over 2,000 years ago.
summary: Comparing the noon Sun in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference remarkably well around 240 BCE.

cards.headline: Around 240 BCE, someone measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: Eratosthenes heard that at Syene, at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down a deep well. At the same moment in Alexandria, farther north, a vertical pole cast a shadow about 7° from vertical, roughly one-fiftieth of a full circle.

cards.headline: From angle to planet
cards.body: If Earth is a sphere, the angle difference means the distance between the cities is one-fiftieth of the way around the globe. Multiply that distance by 50 and you get Earth’s circumference. His answer was remarkably close to the modern value of about 40,000 km.

cards.fact: Greek thinkers already knew Earth was round.
cards.context: During lunar eclipses, Earth’s shadow on the Moon is always curved, the shape only a sphere casts every time.

cards.headline: Earth: measured
learned: He compared noon shadows in two cities
Earth’s curved shadow showed it was round

questions.prompt: What did Eratosthenes compare to estimate Earth’s size?

options.label: The length of a day in two cities
The angle of the noon Sun in two cities
The height of two mountains
options.rationale: He used the Sun’s angle, not mountains.

options.label: The Moon’s shadow during an eclipse
options.rationale: He compared the noon Sun in two cities.

questions.explanation: At noon on the solstice, the Sun was straight overhead at Syene but about 7° off vertical at Alexandria. That difference revealed Earth’s curve.

questions.prompt: The shadow angle was about one-fiftieth of a circle. What did Eratosthenes do next?

options.label: Divided the distance between the cities by 50
options.rationale: That would give a tiny number.

options.label: Measured the well’s depth
options.rationale: The well only showed the Sun was overhead.

options.label: Multiplied the distance between the cities by 50

questions.explanation: If the cities are one-fiftieth of the way around Earth, then 50 times the distance between them gives the full circumference.

questions.prompt: From Level 7: during a lunar eclipse, why does Earth’s curved shadow on the Moon show that Earth is round?

options.label: The Moon is round, so every shadow on it looks curved
options.rationale: A flat disc seen edge-on would cast a straight shadow.

options.label: The Sun is round
options.rationale: The shadow’s shape comes from Earth.

options.label: Only full Moons have curved shadows
options.rationale: The shadow’s curve comes from Earth, not the phase.

options.label: Only a sphere casts a curved shadow every time, from every angle

questions.explanation: In a lunar eclipse, Earth’s shadow falls on the Moon. Its edge is always curved, which only a sphere produces from every direction.
